Invest every week or batch the purchases? Compare fees with the cash waiting to enter

Four graphics compare the same future weekly saving budget under different purchase intervals, including trade fees, waiting cash and the ending combined balance.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 4 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Compare future weekly contributions and fixed purchase fees

Interactive planning lab

Ending investments plus waiting cash, selected interval$66,165.19
Completed purchases at the selected interval130
Selected interval minus weekly ending resources$2,459.79

Equal starting cash and equal new contributions available only at the beginning of each modeled week. One model year contains exactly 52 weeks; four-week purchases therefore mean 13 opportunities per year, not calendar-month purchases. A purchase is scheduled every selected number of weeks. It occurs only when available cash exceeds the fixed fee; the fee is paid from that cash and the rest is invested. Cash earns its weekly-equivalent effective return and assets earn their weekly-equivalent effective return after that week’s purchase. No contribution is borrowed from future weeks. All terminal comparisons include uninvested cash, even when the horizon ends between scheduled purchases. Fractional units, unchanged rates and costless deposits are assumed. No selling, spread, ongoing fund cost, tax, minimum lot, settlement delay or commission-free offer is modeled.

The central idea

A purchase schedule changes transaction costs and time in the market. Compare equal deposits and keep waiting cash in the result before choosing a frequency.

01

These are future contributions, not a lump sum already in hand

The comparison starts with the same initial cash and adds the same contribution at the beginning of every modeled week. Neither strategy borrows contributions from later paycheques. This is a different decision from choosing when to invest a lump sum that already exists.

One strategy purchases every week. The other accumulates cash and purchases at the selected interval. On a scheduled purchase date it pays one fixed fee from the available cash and invests the rest. If cash does not exceed the fee, the purchase is skipped and no fee is charged.

Every model year contains fifty-two weeks. Buying every four weeks therefore creates thirteen scheduled opportunities a year. It does not mean twelve calendar-month purchases. That distinction matters when translating a frequency into a fee total or comparing it with a real payroll and brokerage schedule.

02

A fixed charge can be a large share of a small purchase

Investor.gov distinguishes transaction fees from ongoing investment expenses. This tool focuses on one fixed charge per completed purchase. It excludes annual fund expenses, spreads, exchange charges and other account costs, which would need to be added for a real implementation decision.

The original example contributes CAD 100 weekly for ten fifty-two-week years, with a hypothetical CAD 5 fee per purchase. Buying every week completes 520 trades and pays CAD 2,600 in nominal fees. Buying every four weeks completes 130 trades and pays CAD 650, assuming each scheduled purchase can be funded.

The difference in nominal charges is CAD 1,950. That is not automatically the ending wealth difference: paying a fee also changes the capital left to earn returns, while batching changes how long contributions stay in cash. The first chart therefore compares total resources as well as the fee chart.

03

Waiting money still belongs in the comparison

The third chart shows the first model year’s waiting cash. Contributions arrive, earn the selected cash return when retained, and are transferred on completed purchase dates. The repeated rise and fall can be a planned batching process, rather than evidence of a failed contribution.

At the finish, total resources equal invested asset value plus cash still waiting. This matters when the chosen interval does not divide the number of modeled weeks exactly. A final contribution is not lost merely because the next scheduled purchase is after the horizon.

Initial cash also follows the selected schedule. If a reader enters a large opening amount, it waits until the first scheduled purchase in that strategy. That is an explicit assumption, not a recommendation to delay deploying an existing lump sum. Use zero opening cash to isolate the implementation of future weekly saving.

04

Fee savings and market exposure can pull in different directions

The original example assumes an effective annual asset return of 5% and cash return of 2%, converted to weekly factors. At ten model years, weekly buying ends at approximately CAD 63,705 and four-week buying at approximately CAD 66,165. Both have received the same CAD 52,000 of contributions.

Those are original calculations for a smooth invented return path, not historical strategy results. The asset and cash returns do not fluctuate. A higher asset return can increase the opportunity cost of waiting, while a negative asset return can make delayed exposure beneficial in this particular model. Real markets provide changing prices and uncertain paths.

The fourth chart changes the fee and purchase interval. Every cell subtracts a weekly-purchase strategy with the same row fee and all other selected assumptions. Positive values favour that interval within the cell; negative values favour weekly buying. The matrix does not assign probabilities or identify a universally best trading frequency.

05

Check the full implementation before changing the schedule

A real platform may have commission-free purchases, minimum ticket sizes, fractional-unit restrictions, automatic plans or different charges for different products. The model does not assess the availability, quality or terms of any broker. A zero entered trade fee also does not mean an investment has no ongoing expenses.

Confirm the actual deposit timing, purchase timing, fee schedule, settlement arrangements and treatment of small residual cash. Consider whether the chosen schedule is easy to follow when income changes. An implementation that is hard to maintain can produce a different cash path from the one drawn here.

  1. Hold the saving budget and deposit dates constant.
  2. Count completed purchases rather than only scheduled dates.
  3. Deduct fees from the same resources used to invest.
  4. Include uninvested cash at the comparison date.
  5. Test more than one relationship between asset and cash returns.

The question is how to implement an already appropriate saving plan. A lower transaction bill does not establish that the underlying investment, account or risk level is suitable for the goal.
